title: India Passes Bill to Reintroduce Fees on UPI Merchant Payments
excerpt: After six years of zero charges that fueled the world's largest real-time payment system, New Delhi will allow banks to levy merchant fees on large UPI transactions while keeping person-to-person payments free.
body:
• India passed a bill on August 10 amending the Payment and Settlement Systems Act to allow merchant fees on UPI and RuPay debit card transactions.
  • The proposed merchant discount rate of 0.3–0.5% would apply to large merchant transactions above ₹2,000, which account for just 4% of UPI volume but 67% of total value.
  • Person-to-person payments and small merchant transactions will remain free under the new framework.
  • UPI processed 241.62 billion transactions worth ₹314 lakh crore in FY 2025-26, accounting for 84% of India's retail payment volume.

India's parliament passed a bill on August 10 allowing the reintroduction of merchant fees on transactions processed through the Unified Payments Interface, ending a six-year policy of zero charges that helped UPI grow into the world's largest real-time payment system but left its operators struggling to cover mounting infrastructure costs.

The legislation amends the Payment and Settlement Systems Act of 2007, empowering the government to introduce processing fees or a merchant discount rate on UPI and RuPay debit card transactions through future notifications. The Finance Ministry clarified that person-to-person transactions will remain free and charges will be "threshold based" for a "limited set of merchant transactions."

How the Fees Would Work

Under proposals being considered, banks and payment companies could levy a merchant discount rate of 0.3% to 0.5% on larger transactions at big businesses. The leading proposal would apply charges only to transactions above ₹2,000 — a threshold that captures just 4% of UPI's transaction volume but 67% of its total value, according to government data.

India scrapped the merchant discount rate on UPI transactions in January 2020 to accelerate adoption. The move worked spectacularly: annual UPI volume surged from 12.5 billion transactions in FY 2019-20 to 241.62 billion in FY 2025-26, a 20.3% year-on-year growth rate that has held even at massive scale. But the zero-fee policy left banks and payment service providers absorbing the full cost of infrastructure, settlement, fraud detection, and customer support.

"Someone will have to pay the cost. Ultimately, it is the consumer, in some way or the other, who is paying for it already. It may not be directly on the user-pays principle."

— Sanjay Malhotra, Governor, Reserve Bank of India

Scale That Demands a Revenue Model

At its ten-year mark, UPI's scale is staggering. The system now handles over 23 billion transactions monthly, with July 2026 recording 2,366 crore transactions — the highest single month in its history. Annual transaction value reached approximately ₹314 lakh crore ($3.75 trillion) in FY 2025-26, equivalent to 88% of India's GDP according to an EBANX analysis. The platform has 550 million users across 703 banks.

Yet much of this volume is in small payments. The average UPI transaction has fallen from ₹1,836 during the pandemic to about ₹1,300 by July 2026, reflecting deep penetration into everyday purchases. This is precisely the segment the government wants to shield from fees. Chief Economic Advisor V. Anantha Nageswaran framed the broader principle bluntly, calling free services "the most expensive word in public policy" and noting that infrastructure built on below-cost promises cannot attract patient capital.

A Contentious Move

The fee reintroduction has divided opinion. Reuters described the move as a "necessary good," arguing that merchant charges will ensure the system — propped up by Alphabet's Google Pay, Walmart's PhonePe, and Paytm — continues investing in infrastructure. Supporters argue it introduces what experts call "commercial sanity," allowing market participants to price risk and generate funds for system reliability.

Critics counter that UPI should not be treated as a cost to be recovered. The Hindu Business Line's editorial board noted the move coincides with sustained U.S. pressure over Indian policies that have eroded the businesses of Visa and Mastercard, which typically charge merchants 1–3% per transaction. UPI disrupted that model by enabling direct bank-account transfers via QR code at zero cost to either party. A 2024 survey found 75% of UPI users said they would stop using the service if fees were introduced, though the threshold-based design is meant to avoid that outcome.

What It Means for the Diaspora

UPI now operates in 11 countries including the UAE, Singapore, Qatar, France, and Greece, increasingly serving as a remittance and travel payments channel for the Indian diaspora. Whether the new fee structure extends to cross-border transactions remains to be seen. Brazil's Pix system — which remains free for individuals while charging businesses — offers a precedent that India appears to be following, monetizing high-value merchant flows while keeping the everyday payments rail open.
